newsitem.title: RWANDA: Tutsi fighters attack Zairean city of Goma.
newsitem.headline: Tutsi fighters attack Zairean city of Goma.

text.p: Tutsi fighters attacked near the eastern Zairean city of Goma on Thursday, exchanging mortar and machinegun fire with Zairean forces and sending refugees fleeing.
Aid workers in the North Kivu provincial capital and centre for relief efforts for refugees in eastern Zaire were awoken by firing on the edge of the city in the early morning.

The conflict began with a Zairean army campaign against Tutsis but springs from deadly rivalry between Tutsis and Hutus which killed up to one million people in Rwanda's 1994 genocide and left Zaire hosting 1.1 million Hutu Rwandan refugees.

Incoming and outgoing mortar bombs and heavy weapons fire centred on an area about two km (one mile) north of the city limits and from the Rwandan border I saw mortar bombs explode in the outskirts of Goma.

"There is fire from the Zairean army going north from the airport. We spoke this morning with a Zairean military official who said the rebels have broken through a line at Manigi, 10 km (six miles) outside of Goma," said Steve Pratt, an official with the CARE International agency in Goma speaking by radio.
"The Zairean military official told us we should not worry because the Zaireans would leave the airport and let it be occupied by the other side," he added.

The airport is about five km (three miles) north of the city centre and a key target because aid agencies use it to bring in staff and supplies for refugees and the Zairean military has been bringing in army reinforcements in recent days through it.

Panos Moumtzis, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Goma, confirmed by telephone fighting was raging 10 km (six miles) north of Goma and five km (three miles) from the airport.
"It would seem this is a critical day for the airport. We have heard a lot of noise from around the area," said Moumtzis.

"There is a general feeling of law and order breaking down with two UNHCR vehicles hijacked this morning. Some aid agency compounds and offices have been attacked by Zairean soldiers and looting is under way but it is still limited," he told Reuters.
He said leaders in Kahindo camp north of Goma with some 110,000 residents decided on Wednesday night to pull out towards Mugunga camp, to the west of the city, and had done so at first light.
"There has not been any attack but in the last three or four days they were surrounded by intruders and could hear a lot of fighting from Kibumba camp, which was emptied on Saturday," he said.
"They are now taking a path through the mountains," he said.

"It feels like a war. As of this morning we feel the fighting is very close and the circle is getting tighter. We are very worried about how we can continue humanitarian assistance," said Moumtzis, adding there were no plans yet to evacuate staff.
"Machinegun and rifle fire turned in the last three hours into mortars," said Michelle Quintaglie, spokeswoman for the World Food Programme in Goma. "The situation has deteriorated very rapidly."
She said the first Zairean and Rwandan refugees of the day were starting to arrive in Mugunga, already the world's largest refugee camp crammed with an estimated 400,000 residents.
The Roman Catholic archbishop of the town of Bukavu, south of Goma, was killed on Tuesday and two Spanish priests were separately held hostage in the town under attack from Tutsi rebels.
It was not clear who controlled Bukavu, a lakeside city across from the Rwandan border. Some residents in radio accounts spoke of looting and the presence of Rwandan commandos.
As violence escalated, the special envoy appointed by the United Nations to bring an end to the crisis said on Wednesday he was confident he could get all sides to sit down and talk.
"It's an extraordinarily difficult mission," Raymond Chretien, Canada's ambassador to Washington, told reporters.
Rwanda confirmed on Wednesday some of its troops entered Zaire "after they hit our territory and killed our people."
The Kinshasa government accuses Rwanda and Burundi, whose armies and governments are dominated by Tutsis, of backing the Banyamulenge Tutsis in South Kivu against the Zairean army.
And on Wednesday Zaire for the first time linked Uganda, whose army commanders and Rwanda's were once guerrilla comrades-in-arms, to fresh clashes in its eastern borderlands.
Zaire accuses Rwanda and Burundi, whose armies and governments are dominated by Tutsis, of backing Banyamulenge Tutsis battling its own army.
